ramie.types: Two botanical forms are grown: white ramie (Boehmeria nivea var. nivea), the China grass of temperate East Asia with silvery leaf undersides, and green ramie (var. tenacissima), adapted to the humid tropics. After decortication the raw ribbons are sold as china grass or decorticated ramie, and after degumming as clean fiber ready for spinning. Degummed fiber is combed into long top for fine, lustrous worsted-type yarns, while the short noil goes into coarser yarns or is cottonized for blending. Yarn quality is judged by fineness, the thoroughness of degumming, whiteness and hairiness. Traditional handwoven ramie cloths include Japan's Ojiya-chijimi and Echigo-jofu and Korea's Hansan mosi.
ramie.fabrics: Pure ramie is woven into crisp, lustrous plain weaves for summer shirts, dresses, table linen and traditional East Asian garments, where fine ramie gauze was valued for hot, humid summers. Blends are more common in Western retail: ramie and cotton knits for sweaters and T-shirts, ramie and linen shirting, and ramie with viscose or silk for drapier cloth. Ramie is also used in canvas, upholstery, fishing lines and nets, industrial sewing thread, and papers where high strength and wet resistance are needed. Its stiffness makes it useful in blends that must hold shape, such as structured jackets.
ramie.quality: Good ramie fabric is smooth, bright and even, without a prickly surface of protruding fiber ends, which indicates coarse or poorly degummed fiber. Rub it against the inside of your wrist to check. High luster and whiteness in undyed cloth reflect thorough degumming and bleaching. Check the content line, because ramie blends are often marketed as linen-look and ramie may not be called linen. In knits, ramie adds crispness but can lose shape and stretch at elbows if the ramie share is high. Heavier, tighter weaves resist the fiber's tendency to break at sharp creases better than loosely woven gauze.
pros: It is among the strongest plant fibers and is at least as strong wet as dry.
It has a natural luster that brightens dyed and undyed cloth.
It absorbs moisture and dries quickly, feeling cool in summer.
It holds its shape and resists shrinking in woven fabrics.
cons: It is stiff and inextensible, so it wrinkles readily and can crack at sharp, repeated folds.
Poorly degummed ramie feels prickly against the skin.
Degumming requires chemical or enzymatic processing with an environmental cost.
Pure ramie is a niche fabric, so supply and documentation can be limited outside East Asia.
ramie.impact: Ramie is a perennial that can be cut several times a year from the same roots, which reduces tillage, but its main environmental issue is degumming. Removing roughly a quarter to a third of the ribbon's mass as gums conventionally means boiling in alkali, then bleaching and washing, producing strong effluent that needs treatment; enzymatic and microbial degumming aims to cut those loads but is not yet the norm. Independent, dated life cycle assessments of ramie fabric are scarce, so claims of a low footprint should be treated with caution. China is the main producer and processor, which concentrates both expertise and supply-chain risk. Degummed ramie is nearly pure cellulose and biodegradable if not coated.
ramie.care: Wash ramie at 30 to 40 C with a mild detergent on a gentle cycle, and dry ramie and cotton sweaters flat so they do not stretch. Avoid wringing and heavy spinning, which set sharp creases that can crack the stiff fiber over time. Line dry woven pieces and remove them while slightly damp. Pure ramie takes a hot iron, about 200 C, best with steam while damp, much like linen; reduce the heat for blends. Avoid chlorine bleach on colors. Store garments hung or loosely rolled rather than folded tightly along the same lines, and keep them dry to prevent mildew.
faq: Ramie is a bast fiber from the stems of Boehmeria nivea, a nettle-family plant long grown in East Asia. It is spun into crisp, lustrous yarns similar to linen and is sold alone or blended with cotton, linen, viscose or silk.
Why were ramie and cotton sweaters so common in the 1980s?

Under US textile import quotas of the period, garments made mostly of ramie were not subject to quota limits, so importers used ramie-majority blends. Congress ended ramie's quota-free status in 1986, and ramie blends became less common afterward.

Well-degummed, finely spun ramie feels smooth and cool. Coarse or insufficiently degummed ramie leaves stiff fiber ends protruding from the yarn, which can feel prickly. Blending with cotton and enzyme finishing reduce the effect.
Is ramie the same as linen?

No. Ramie comes from Boehmeria nivea and linen from flax, Linum usitatissimum. They look and behave similarly, but ramie is typically more lustrous and stiffer, and US and EU labeling rules require each to be named correctly.
notable: Garments of more than 50% ramie entered the United States without quota limits until legislation in 1986 ended ramie's quota-free status.
Ramie can be harvested several times a year from the same perennial rootstock.
